elements.name: Main Program and Subroutines
elements.what: A single main program drives the system by calling a hierarchy of subroutines, with control returning up the call tree after each call.
elements.problem: How to organize a computation-dominant system when the decomposition follows functional refinement; correctness of a component depends only on the subroutines it calls, but data flow through shared parameters/globals resists change.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

elements.name: Object-Oriented Organization
elements.what: The system is organized as a collection of abstract-data-type instances (objects) that hide their representations and interact by invoking each other's operations.
elements.problem: How to localize the effects of representation change; encapsulation lets internals evolve freely, at the cost that every caller must know the identity of the object it invokes.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

elements.name: Event-Based Implicit Invocation
elements.what: Components announce (broadcast) events instead of invoking procedures directly; the system implicitly invokes every procedure registered as interested in that event.
elements.problem: How to integrate components without hard-wiring caller-callee identities; announcers gain strong decoupling but surrender control over which handlers run, in what order, and whether they run at all.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

elements.name: Layered System
elements.what: The system is organized as a hierarchy of layers, each providing services to the layer above and acting as a client of the layer below, ideally hiding all layers beneath it.
elements.problem: How to structure a system so each level of abstraction can be designed, understood, and replaced against the interface of the level below; strict layering conflicts with performance and with functions that cut across levels.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

elements.name: Repository (Shared Data) Style
elements.what: A central data structure represents the system state while a collection of independent components operate on it, coordinating only through the shared store.
elements.problem: How to let many computations cooperate on a large, evolving body of data without direct coupling; the choice of who triggers whom (transactions vs. store state) splits the style into database and blackboard variants.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)
elements.borderline: Same NAME as the design-realm 'repository' (Fowler data-access pattern) - different mechanism, both kept per the same-name-two-realms rule; id suffixed.

elements.name: Blackboard
elements.what: A repository variant in which independent knowledge sources opportunistically react to changes in a shared blackboard data structure, with control emerging from the blackboard state itself.
elements.problem: How to attack problems with no deterministic solution algorithm (speech recognition, signal interpretation) by letting partial results from heterogeneous specialists incrementally converge on a solution.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

elements.name: Interpreter (Architectural Style)
elements.what: The system is organized as a virtual machine: an interpretation engine, the pseudo-program it executes, and the engine's and program's state, closing the gap between the execution platform and the desired semantics.
elements.problem: How to execute programs for a machine that does not exist in hardware, or to make behavior data-driven and portable; the extra level of interpretation trades performance for flexibility.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)
elements.borderline: Same NAME as the design-realm GoF 'interpreter' pattern - the architectural style structures a whole system as a virtual machine; both kept, id suffixed.

elements.name: Rule-Based System
elements.what: An interpreter specialization in which a rule engine (inference/interpretation engine) selects and fires condition-action rules from a knowledge base against working memory.
elements.problem: How to keep volatile domain logic out of code so domain experts can evolve behavior as rules; control flow becomes emergent from rule selection rather than explicit.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

elements.name: Pipes and Filters
elements.what: Independent filters incrementally transform streams of data flowing through connecting pipes, each filter reading inputs and producing outputs with no shared state or knowledge of its neighbors.
elements.problem: How to compose stream transformations so components can be understood, reused, and recombined independently and run concurrently; forces the whole computation into a lowest-common-denominator stream format and can cost parsing/unparsing overhead.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

elements.name: Batch Sequential
elements.what: A degenerate data-flow organization in which each processing step runs to completion on the entire data set before passing the complete result to the next step.
elements.problem: How to structure data processing when steps need the whole input (or when interactive incremental flow is unnecessary); loses the incremental delivery and concurrency of pipes-and-filters but simplifies each stage.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

elements.name: Process Control (Feedback Control Loop)
elements.what: The system is organized around a control loop: a controller reads process variables from sensors, compares them to set points, and adjusts manipulated variables to keep a physical or continuing process on target.
elements.problem: How to maintain specified properties of an ongoing process in the face of external disturbances that cannot be predicted, using open- vs closed-loop and feedback vs feedforward variants; the architecture must make the loop, not the call graph, the primary structure.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Perspectives on an Emerging Discipline - Shaw & Garlan (1996)

elements.name: Client-Server
elements.what: Server components provide services at known locations while client components initiate requests for them, typically via remote procedure call or request/response protocols, with the server unaware of client identities in advance.
elements.problem: How to share centralized resources and services among many distributed consumers; centralizes state and administration at the cost of a scalability and availability bottleneck at the server.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

elements.name: Distributed Processes
elements.what: The system is a set of independent processes, typically on multiple processors, interacting by message passing under some topological organization (ring, star, arbitrary graph).
elements.problem: How to structure systems whose components are inherently concurrent and physically distributed; the architecture must state both the topology and the communication protocol because no shared state exists.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

elements.name: State Transition System (Architectural Organization)
elements.what: A whole reactive system is organized as a set of states plus named transitions that move the system between them, making the state machine the top-level structure rather than an internal mechanism.
elements.problem: How to give reactive/real-time systems an analyzable top-level structure whose behavior can be enumerated and verified; differs from an in-component FSM by governing system organization, not one module's logic.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)
elements.borderline: Names the same idea as the design-realm finite state machine at a different altitude; kept per same-name-two-realms rule as the system-level organization, prime Phase 3b bridge target for the design-realm FSM cluster.

elements.name: Domain-Specific Software Architecture
elements.what: A reference structure specialized to one application domain (e.g. avionics, vehicle management) that fixes the component types, coordination model, and configuration rules that products in that domain instantiate.
elements.problem: How to exploit deep domain regularities for reuse and generation across a product family, trading generality for the power to derive concrete systems (semi-)automatically from the architecture.
elements.named_in: An Introduction to Software Architecture - Garlan & Shaw (1993)

elements.name: C2
elements.what: A layered, message-based style in which components communicate only through explicit connectors via asynchronous notifications (downward) and requests (upward), under a strict substrate-independence rule: a component may know services above it but nothing below.
elements.problem: How to build flexible, distributable GUI-centric systems from reusable off-the-shelf components whose parts can be replaced or rewired at runtime; requires all interaction to be mediated, prohibiting direct component links and shared address-space assumptions.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

elements.name: REST (Representational State Transfer)
elements.what: A hybrid network-based style constraining client-server interaction to be stateless, cacheable, layered, and mediated by a uniform interface over resources identified by URIs and manipulated via exchanged representations, optionally extended by code-on-demand.
elements.problem: How to make an Internet-scale hypermedia system evolvable, scalable, and visible to intermediaries; the constraints trade per-interaction efficiency (self-descriptive messages, statelessness) for anarchic scalability and independent deployment of components.
elements.named_in: Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures - Fielding (2000)

elements.name: Peer-to-Peer
elements.what: Networked components (peers) act as both clients and servers of one another, discovering and exchanging services directly without a distinguished central server.
elements.problem: How to achieve scalability, resilience, and resource pooling when no node can be trusted or provisioned as a permanent center; pays for decentralization with discovery, consistency, and trust problems.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

elements.name: Publish-Subscribe (Architectural Style)
elements.what: Publishers emit messages classified by topic or content to an intermediary event service, which delivers them to all components that have subscribed, so producers and consumers never address each other.
elements.problem: How to decouple many-to-many information flow in space, time, and synchronization across a distributed system; delivery ordering, reliability, and subscription management move into the connector.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)
elements.borderline: Same NAME as the design realm's in-process publish-subscribe (observer / event-aggregator / publish-subscribe-channel); this is the system-scale style with a distributed event service - both kept, id suffixed.

elements.name: Distributed Objects
elements.what: System functionality is partitioned into objects whose methods can be invoked across process and machine boundaries through proxies and an object request broker, preserving OO interfaces over the network.
elements.problem: How to extend object-oriented organization to distributed systems while hiding location and transport; masks but does not remove the latency, partial-failure, and concurrency differences between local and remote calls.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

elements.name: N-Tier Client-Server
elements.what: Client-server generalized to a chain of tiers (e.g. presentation, business logic, data management), each acting as server to the tier before it and client of the tier after it, deployable on separate machines.
elements.problem: How to scale, secure, and independently evolve the presentation, application, and data concerns of an enterprise system; each added tier buys isolation and scaling at the price of latency and deployment complexity.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

elements.name: Sense-Compute-Control
elements.what: An embedded-systems organization structured as a repeating loop of sensor reading, computation over the sensed values plus internal state, and actuator commands controlling the environment.
elements.problem: How to structure reactive embedded software whose primary job is continuous interaction with physical hardware; keeps timing and I/O concerns explicit at the top level rather than buried in a call hierarchy.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

elements.name: Code-on-Demand
elements.what: A mobile-code style in which a client that has the data and processing resources requests executable code (know-how) from a remote server and runs it locally, as with scripts delivered to a browser.
elements.problem: How to extend a deployed client's functionality without redeployment, moving computation to where the data and interaction are; introduces trust, versioning, and sandboxing obligations on the receiving site.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

elements.name: Remote Evaluation
elements.what: A mobile-code style in which a component that has the know-how sends code to a remote site that has the resources and data, where it executes and returns results.
elements.problem: How to bring computation to remote data or special resources instead of shipping bulk data to the computation; the receiving site must safely execute foreign code and account for its resource use.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

elements.name: Mobile Agent
elements.what: A mobile-code style in which an entire computational unit - code, execution state, and data - migrates itself from site to site, resuming execution at each destination.
elements.problem: How to sustain a long-lived computation across intermittently connected or resource-shifting hosts; state capture, migration transparency, and security of both agent and host dominate the design.
elements.named_in: Software Architecture: Foundations, Theory, and Practice - Taylor, Medvidovic & Dashofy (2010)

elements.name: Procedure Call Connector
elements.what: A connector that transfers control and data between components through invocation with parameters and (usually) a return, spanning local calls, method invocations, callbacks, and system calls.
elements.problem: How to couple components when the caller needs the callee's result before proceeding; the dominant, best-understood interaction primitive, but synchronous and identity-coupled by default.
elements.named_in: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

elements.name: Event Connector
elements.what: A connector that transfers control and data by delivering occurrences (events) from producers to registered observers, with dimensions for cardinality, delivery guarantees, synchronicity, and notification mode.
elements.problem: How to interact without the initiator knowing or waiting on the recipients; decouples identity and time, but delivery ordering, loss, and causality become connector-level design decisions.
elements.named_in: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

elements.name: Data Access Connector
elements.what: A connector through which a component reads or writes data maintained by a data store or another component, covering repository access, database queries, and accessor operations, often with translation/conversion.
elements.problem: How to mediate interaction that flows through persistent or shared state rather than control transfer; transactionality, locality, and format conversion are the governing forces.
elements.named_in: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

elements.name: Linkage Connector
elements.what: A connector that ties system elements together by establishing and enforcing associations - name bindings, imports/exports, and compile- or load-time linking - enabling other connectors to act at runtime.
elements.problem: How components come to be composed at all: the facilitation of later interaction; linkage decisions (static vs dynamic, granularity of binding) fix how late a system can be reconfigured.
elements.named_in: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

elements.name: Stream Connector
elements.what: A connector that transfers sequences of data between autonomous processes, covering pipes, sockets, and other bounded/unbounded, buffered, structured or raw data flows.
elements.problem: How to move large or continuous data between concurrently executing components; buffering, throughput, ordering, and blocking behavior are the connector's defining choices.
elements.named_in: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

elements.name: Arbitrator Connector
elements.what: A connector that resolves conflicts and redirects control among components with conflicting needs, providing concurrency control (locks, semaphores), scheduling, load balancing, and fault-handling negotiation.
elements.problem: How to coordinate components that contend for shared resources or must agree despite failures; centralizes the coordination policy in the connector instead of scattering it through components.
elements.named_in: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

elements.name: Adaptor Connector
elements.what: A connector that converts between mismatched interaction policies, interfaces, or data formats of components not designed to interoperate - wrappers, transformers, and protocol converters.
elements.problem: How to compose heterogeneous or independently developed components whose assumptions disagree; conversion cost and semantic fidelity of the mapping are the central forces.
elements.named_in: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)
elements.borderline: Same NAME family as the design-realm GoF Adapter pattern; the connector type is the architecture-level interaction mediator - both kept per same-name-two-realms rule.

elements.name: Distributor Connector
elements.what: A connector that identifies interaction paths and routes communication among components - naming, registration/lookup, and delivery services such as DNS-style naming, routing, and multicast distribution.
elements.problem: How interacting parties find each other and how messages reach them across a topology; never used alone, it composes with procedure-call or stream connectors to form RPCs and distributed messaging.
elements.named_in: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors - Mehta, Medvidovic & Phadke (2000)

rejected.name: Heterogeneous Architectures
rejected.why: Garlan-Shaw 3.8 is a meta-observation (styles combine hierarchically, per-component, or by elaboration), not a specific bridgeable structure; a catch-all node is worthless by mission rule.

rejected.name: Virtual Machine (as separate style)
rejected.why: Garlan-Shaw and TMD treat interpreters and virtual machines as one organization ('virtual machines' is TMD's group label for interpreter/mobile-code/rule-based); aka recorded on interpreter-style.

rejected.name: Event Notification (TMD style entry)
rejected.why: TMD's 'event-based' style is the same mechanism Garlan-Shaw name event-based implicit invocation; the distributed many-to-many variant with an event service is publish-subscribe-style.

rejected.name: Pipeline
rejected.why: Linear specialization of pipes-and-filters (Garlan-Shaw name it as such); recorded as aka.

rejected.name: RPC (Remote Procedure Call) as connector element
rejected.why: In the Mehta-Medvidovic-Phadke taxonomy RPC is a composite species (procedure call + distributor), not a ninth basic type; recorded as aka on procedure-call-connector, composition noted on distributor-connector.

rejected.name: Communication / Coordination / Conversion / Facilitation (connector service categories)
rejected.why: The four service categories are classification dimensions of the taxonomy, not connector types; the eight types are the elements.

rejected.name: KWIC solutions / compiler / Hearsay-II / cruise-control case studies
rejected.why: Shaw-Garlan case studies are exemplars illustrating the styles, not elements.

rejected.name: Fielding's intermediate derived styles (client-stateless-server, layered-client-server, etc.)
rejected.why: Constraint-composition waypoints on the derivation path to REST, not independently used styles; REST itself is cataloged.

notes: Verification: Garlan & Shaw 1993 loaded live from CMU (sections 3.1-3.8 confirmed verbatim: Pipes and Filters; Data Abstraction and Object-Oriented Organization; Event-based Implicit Invocation; Layered Systems; Repositories; Table Driven Interpreters; Other Familiar Architectures = distributed processes, main program/subroutine, state transition systems, process control systems, domain-specific software architectures; Heterogeneous Architectures; 'batch sequential' named in-text). Mehta-Medvidovic-Phadke ICSE 2000 loaded live (all 8 connector types + 4 service categories confirmed). Corpus ids used: garlanshaw93, shawgarlan96, tmd (Taylor-Medvidovic-Dashofy 2010 IS in work_ids.tsv as 'tmd'). Pass-8 addendum candidates (named_in_corpus_id=null): Fielding 2000 dissertation (names REST; TMD is the corpus treatment); Mehta-Medvidovic-Phadke 2000 'Towards a Taxonomy of Software Connectors' (names the 8 connector types; TMD ch.5 is the corpus treatment). Cross-scout merge expectations: layered-style/pipes-and-filters/blackboard/client-server/publish-subscribe-style will also surface from the POSA1 and Bass scouts - fold on merge, keep these ids or theirs, one node per style. Design-realm name collisions handled with suffixed ids per rule: repository-style, interpreter-style, publish-subscribe-style; state-transition-system and adaptor-connector flagged borderline for the same reason. C2's primary naming source (Taylor et al. 1996 ICSE paper) cited via tmd, its book treatment - if the merge wants the primary paper, it is a further pass-8 candidate.
